summary: Levonorgestrel is a synthetic second-generation progestin used most commonly as a single 1.5 mg dose for emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse, and also in progestin-only pills, combined oral contraceptives and intrauterine systems. It works mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation; it is not effective and is not indicated once a pregnancy has been established and does not cause abortion. It is well tolerated, the main effects being menstrual changes, nausea and headache.
indications: Emergency contraception to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure (single 1.5 mg dose)
Progestin-only oral contraception (continuous low-dose, separate product)
Component of combined oral contraceptives (with ethinyl estradiol) for routine contraception
Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system for long-acting contraception and (some products) heavy menstrual bleeding

moa: Levonorgestrel is a progestogen that acts principally by inhibiting or delaying the luteinizing hormone surge, thereby preventing or postponing ovulation. It may also thicken cervical mucus to impede sperm transport. When used for emergency contraception its main effect is preventing ovulation/fertilization; it is not effective once implantation has begun and does not interrupt an established pregnancy.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to levonorgestrel or any component
Undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding (for ongoing progestin contraception)
relative: Severe hepatic disease or hepatic tumor
History of, or risk factors for, ectopic pregnancy
Active venous thromboembolism (for ongoing progestin use)
monitor: Recurrent need for emergency contraception (consider regular method)

preg: Levonorgestrel is not for use during pregnancy and is ineffective once a pregnancy is established; it does not cause abortion. Epidemiologic data have not shown an increased risk of birth defects from inadvertent exposure. Discontinue ongoing progestin contraception if pregnancy occurs.
lact: Small amounts of levonorgestrel are excreted in breast milk; it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding and is not expected to harm the infant. For ongoing progestin contraception, progestin-only methods are preferred over combined products during lactation.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required for emergency-contraception use in renal impairment. Use according to clinical judgment.
hepatic: Avoid in acute liver disease, active hepatitis or hepatic tumors. Hepatic enzyme induction can reduce efficacy. Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Hepatic enzyme inducers (rifampin, rifabutin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, efavirenz, St. John's wort) - accelerate levonorgestrel metabolism and reduce contraceptive efficacy
moderate: Ulipristal acetate - levonorgestrel may reduce its efficacy if taken together (do not combine emergency-contraception agents)
HIV protease inhibitors / certain antiretrovirals - may alter progestin levels
minor: Antacids/other drugs - no clinically significant interaction reported
interactions.food: No significant food interaction; take without regard to meals.
interactions.diagnostics: May affect certain endocrine and liver function laboratory parameters; menstrual timing may be altered.

common: Menstrual changes (earlier, later, heavier or lighter bleeding)
serious: Ectopic pregnancy (if pregnancy occurs despite use)
emergency: Signs of ectopic pregnancy (severe lower abdominal pain, especially 3-5 weeks after use)

Evaluate for ectopic pregnancy if severe lower abdominal pain occurs
For ongoing progestin contraception: blood pressure, menstrual pattern and adherence

pearls: Single 1.5 mg dose is the preferred emergency-contraception regimen and is more effective the earlier it is taken (ideally within 72 hours)
It works mainly by delaying ovulation and does NOT terminate an established pregnancy - it is not an abortifacient
Efficacy is reduced in higher-weight individuals; ulipristal acetate or a copper IUD may be more effective options
Enzyme-inducing drugs (rifampin, certain anticonvulsants, St. John's wort) markedly reduce efficacy - a copper IUD is preferred in such patients

openFDA returns levonorgestrel chiefly within combined oral contraceptive labels (e.g. with ethinyl estradiol); this record reflects standalone levonorgestrel (emergency/progestin-only) use - verify against the specific product labeling
missed: For single-dose emergency contraception there is no missed-dose concept - take it as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse. For ongoing progestin-only contraception, a pill more than 3 hours late is considered missed: take it as soon as remembered and use back-up contraception for 48 hours per product instructions.
overdose: No serious adverse effects from overdose of oral contraceptive/progestin products have been reported, including in children. Overdose may cause nausea and, in females, withdrawal bleeding. Treatment is supportive; no specific antidote is required.
